newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Tutu tut-tuts Mandela live-in lover deal.
newsitem.headline: Tutu tut-tuts Mandela live-in lover deal.

text.p: Most South Africans are delighted that divorced President Nelson Mandela has taken a live-in lover, but Archbishop Desmond Tutu is among those who think he ought to marry his elegant Mozambican sweetheart.
For the past year, Mandela tried to keep the affair secret, sometimes meeting his love in remote game lodges on the border between their countries.

But at the weekend, on his boss's orders, spokesman Parks Mankahlana proved high society gossips right when he confirmed that Mandela, 78, and Mozambique's former first lady Graca Machel, 50, planned to live together for half of every month.
"They will try to arrange to be together for two weeks of every month. Mrs Machel will come to him, whether he is in Cape Town or Johannesburg," he told Reuters later.
Public reaction was immediatley positive.
But church leaders including Tutu, the 1984 Nobel Peace Prize laureate and retired head of the Anglican Church in Southern Africa, have expressed reservations.

Mandela telephoned Tutu, senior party leaders and some provincial premiers last week to warn them he was about to go public about his love life, sources in his ruling African National Congress (ANC) party told Reuters.
"The archbishop told Mr Mandela to think about the example he would be setting to the nation's children," one source said. "He told him he should rather get married," said another.
Kenneth Meshoe of the African Christian Democratic Party also criticised the president's informal solution, saying this would encourage cohabitation in black society.
"This relationship is not setting a good example. Mandela is a national leader and an international leader. People look up to him and say if he does it, it must be right," he said.

In an interview in Maputo earlier this week, Graca Machel, whose late husband Samora liberated Mozambique from Portuguese colonial rule, said she and Mandela had already made up their minds that marriage was not on the cards.

South Africa's Chief Rabbi Cyril Harris said he was delighted for Mandela, adding: "People are entitled to their happiness and Judaism would say it is far, far better for two people to be together than to be lonely."
Catholic Archbishop Lawrence Henry said only: "As both are national figures, I am confident that whatever they decide on, their future together will be done with careful consideration."

Sowetan, the country's top-selling black daily commented in an editorial: "President Nelson Mandela has the right to enjoy the twilight years of his life in happiness and in this regard his relationship with Graca Machel is most welcome."
The newspaper seemed to reflect popular feeling in radio phone-ins and informal newspaper polls, where most said Mandela deserves some personal happiness.
Mandela's first marriage collapsed before he was jailed in 1962 for fighting apartheid and his second, to Winnie Mandela, ended in March in a messy and painful divorce.
"Ever since I came back from jail (in 1990), not once has the defendant ever entered the bedroom while I was awake," Mandela told the divorce court earlier this year.
Graca Machel, whose husband died in a plane crash on the border with South Africa in 1986, is a respected academic and a tireless ambassador for the rights of the world's children.
ANC and opposition legislators told Reuters she would make a perfect first lady for the man who is loved by almost every South African and whom some call "Saint Nelson".

Back in Mozambique on Wednesday after a visit with Mandela to his childhood home in the rural Eastern Cape town of Qunu, Machel acknowledged that she and Mandela had an "amorous" relationship, but a wedding was out.
"I will always be the wife of Samora Machel. I like being called Mrs Machel. It's the only way I can keep my husband alive," she said.
